Welcome to our Developer Guidelines. This document outlines the foundational technical standards and best practices defined by our engineering leadership. Adhering to these guidelines ensures consistency, security, and scalability across all our systems. Below is a concise overview of our core technical policies: Phone Number Format: Mandatory storage using the international E.164 standard (e.g., +1234567890), saved as a String without spaces, hyphens, or special characters to ensure compatibility with SMS and telephony providers. Allowed Encryption Algorithms: Exclusive use of high-security industry standards, such as AES-256 for data at rest and TLS 1.2 or higher for data in transit. Disallowed Encryption Algorithms: Strict prohibition of obsolete, insecure, or vulnerable algorithms such as MD5, SHA-1, DES, or 3DES for any authentication, hashing, or data protection processes. Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS): Strict prohibition of wildcard origins (*) in production environments. Allowed origins must be explicitly whitelisted, and the Access-Control-Allow-Credentials header must only be set to true when combined with specific, trusted origins. Date and Time Management: Mandatory storage in the UTC timezone and communication using the ISO 8601 standard. API Design and Versioning: Rules for URL structuring, pagination handling, and mandatory endpoint versioning (e.g., /v1/users). Secrets Management: Strict prohibition of hardcoded credentials in the source code and mandatory use of vault managers (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault). Log Structure: Requirement to record events in a structured format (such as JSON), standardizing logging levels (INFO, DEBUG, ERROR) and defining rules for masking Personally Identifiable Information (PII). Authentication and Authorization: Definition of the exact protocols to be used for sessions and third-party integrations (e.g., JWT, OAuth 2.0, SAML). Error Handling: A unified structure (a standard JSON payload) for returning error messages to the client, strictly avoiding the exposure of database or server traces (stack traces). Identifier (ID) Strategy: Guidelines on when to use UUIDs/GUIDs (unique alphanumeric strings) versus auto-incrementing integer IDs in our databases. Data Deletion (Soft vs. Hard Delete): Rules defining which type of information can be physically deleted from the database (hard delete) and which must only be marked as inactive for audit and compliance purposes (soft delete). Quality Thresholds (CI/CD Gates): Mandatory minimum percentage for test coverage (e.g., 80%) and passing static code analysis (e.g., SonarQube) required before allowing any deployment to production. Currency and Money Management: Requirement to store monetary values in their smallest unit (e.g., cents as integers) to prevent precision errors associated with floating-point decimals. Injection Vulnerabilities Prevention: Strict requirement to prevent injection attacks (SQL, NoSQL, and Command Injection) by utilizing parameterized queries, prepared statements, ORM/ODM built-in sanitization, and rigorous input validation. Raw query concatenation using untrusted user input is strictly prohibited. Error Handling and Stack Traces: Mandatory filtering of all backend errors before they reach the client. Production environments must return generic, user-friendly error messages using a unified JSON payload, strictly forbidding the exposure of application stack traces, database schemas, or internal server details. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) and Permissions: Mandatory implementation of the Principle of Least Privilege. Access to resources, APIs, and administrative functionalities must be strictly restricted based on explicitly defined user roles and permissions, verified server-side on every request. Secure Token Storage (Cookies vs. LocalStorage): Sensitive authentication tokens (such as JWTs or session IDs) must never be stored in LocalStorage or SessionStorage due to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) risks. They must be stored in secure, server-side cookies configured with the HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite=Strict (or Lax) attributes. Rate Limiting and Retry Restrictions: Strict enforcement of maximum retry thresholds for sensitive operations. Rate limiting must be implemented to prevent brute-force attacks on login endpoints (failed passwords) and to mitigate fraud or systemic abuse in online payment processing and checkout flows. Dependency Versioning and Security: Strict prohibition of using the latest tag or loose version ranges (e.g., wildcards) for third-party libraries and package dependencies. All dependencies must be pinned to a fixed, explicit version (and locked via lockfiles like package-lock.json, go.sum, or Gemfile.lock) to avoid unexpected breaking changes and mitigate supply chain security attacks. Country and Subdivision Identification (ISO 3166): Mandatory use of the ISO 3166 standard for geographical codes. Country codes must follow ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 (e.g., US, ES, CO), and regional subdivisions like states, provinces, or departments must follow ISO 3166-2 (e.g., US-NY for New York, ES-B for Barcelona, CO-DC for Bogotá) to ensure data normalization across all databases and integrations. Location and Port Identification (UN/LOCODE): Mandatory use of the United Nations Code for Trade and Transport Locations (UN/LOCODE) standard (e.g., USNYC for New York, ESBCN for Barcelona) when storing, identifying, or transmitting data related to cities, ports, and international trade hubs across logistics and global operations.

Country Code Top-Level Domains (ISO 3166-1 ccTLD): Mandatory use of official country-specific domain suffixes (e.g., .co, .mx, .es) for localized routing and web infrastructure management [Schema/Field: cctld]. Media and File Types (MIME Type): Requirement to explicitly define and validate file formats using standard Internet media types (e.g., application/json, image/png) during upload and transit [Schema/Field: mime_type]. Credit Card PAN (ISO/IEC 7813): Primary Account Numbers (PAN) for credit/debit cards must adhere to standard structural lengths and formatting (e.g., 4111111111111111) before processing or masking [Schema/Field: card_pan]. Product Barcodes (EAN-13 / GTIN): Global Trade Item Numbers and retail barcodes must strictly follow the 13-digit international serialization format (e.g., 7702009119429) [Schema/Field: gtin or barcode]. Language Codes (ISO 639-1): Mandatory use of the two-letter lowercase format (e.g., es, en, pt) for identifying primary application languages [Schema/Field: language_code]. System Locales (BCP 47): Identification of regional and cultural formatting defaults must follow the hyphenated language-region format (e.g., es-CO, en-US) [Schema/Field: locale]. Extended Locales (Unicode CLDR): Internal localization libraries and database locales requiring strict structural formatting must utilize the underscore-separated Common Locale Data Repository format (e.g., es_CO) [Schema/Field: cldr_locale].
A short list of practices that help a small team move fast without breaking things.
documents.s: Best Practices for a Startup Software Team

documents.t: Feature flags let you deploy code without releasing it. Merge code often, even if the feature is not finished. Use flags as a kill switch: turn a feature off without a new deploy. Give each flag an owner and a removal date. Delete the flag after the full rollout.

Use one engine to manage flags and settings for all services. One source of truth, with values per environment (dev, staging, production). Keep an audit log of who changed what and when. Use an existing tool (for example Unleash, OpenFeature, or LaunchDarkly) before building your own.

Do not build and release a whole feature at once. Break it into small phases that each give value and can work alone. Ship each phase behind its own flag and turn it on step by step (team, then a small percentage of users, then everyone). Smaller changes are easier to review, test, and roll back.

A postmortem is only useful if the fixes happen. Create a ticket for every action item, with an owner and a due date. Put these tickets in the normal backlog and planning, not in a separate list. Review open action items regularly.
documents.s: 4. Turn postmortem action items into tasks

documents.t: Keep related services and shared code in one repository. Share code and tools easily, and change several packages in one pull request. One CI setup and one set of standards for everyone. Tools like Nx, Turborepo, or Bazel keep builds fast as the repo grows.

Frameworks such as NestJS or Ruby on Rails have a fixed structure, so everyone writes code in a similar way. Less debate about folders, naming, and patterns. New people learn the project faster. If you use a flexible technology, write the conventions down clearly and enforce them with linters, templates, and code review.

AI tools work better when they understand the project. Describe the folder structure, the architecture, and the main conventions. Keep it in the repo (for example AGENTS.md or docs/architecture.md) and update it with the code. Good documentation for AI is also good documentation for new teammates.
documents.s: 7. Document the code structure for AI from day one

documents.t: Write one document per feature that explains everything needed to turn it on. List the feature flags and configurations to add, and in which order to enable them. List the services and dependencies involved. Link it from the pull requests and the rollout plan. Simple template: # Feature: <name> - Goal: <one sentence> - Phases: <phase 1, phase 2, ...> - Feature flags: <flag name -> what it controls> - Configurations: <key -> value per environment> - Services involved: <list> - Rollout steps: <order to enable each flag> - Rollback: <how to turn it off>

When an urgent support escalation lands and an immediate fix is not feasible, pull the metrics first. Query your logs, metrics, or database to determine exactly how many users or workflows are actually affected. What feels critical to a single vocal customer often turns out to have a very low blast radius across the broader platform. Concrete numbers eliminate urgency theater and knee-jerk patching, giving the engineering team composure to build the right solution. Share the verified impact data with Support and stakeholders to set realistic expectations and handle the situation calmly.

documents.t: This document provides useful queries for AWS CloudWatch logs to filter and sort error messages.
fields @timestamp, @message, @logStream, @log | filter @message like 'uncaughtException' | sort @timestamp desc | limit 10000

This query retrieves log entries containing the term 'uncaughtException'. Here’s a breakdown of the command: fields @timestamp, @message, @logStream, @log: Specifies the fields to be displayed in the results. @timestamp: The time when the log entry was created. @message: The content of the log entry. @logStream: The stream from which the log entry originates. @log: The log group associated with the entry. filter @message like 'uncaughtException': Filters the log entries to include only those that contain the specified term. sort @timestamp desc: Sorts the results by timestamp in descending order, showing the most recent entries first. limit 10000: Limits the number of returned entries to 10,000.
fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like 'SOME_ERROR' | stats count() as total_matches
documents.s: Filter Log Messages and Count Matches

documents.t: This command filters log messages to identify occurrences of a specific error and counts the total matches. Below is a breakdown of the command: fields @timestamp, @message: Specifies the fields to include in the output, in this case, the timestamp and message. filter @message like 'SOME_ERROR': Filters log messages that contain the string "SOME_ERROR". stats count() as total_matches: Aggregates the filtered results and provides the count of occurrences, labeling the output as total_matches.
fields @message | stats count (*) as total, sum(strlen(@message))/1024/1024 as size by label, level, message | sort by size desc

This query counts the total number of messages and calculates their size, grouped by specific labels, levels, and messages. The following components detail the query's functionality: fields @message: Specifies the field to analyze, which in this case is the message content. stats count (*) as total: Computes the total count of messages and labels it as total. sum(strlen(@message))/1024/1024 as size: Calculates the total size of messages in megabytes by summing the length of each message and converting the result from bytes to megabytes. by label, level, message: Groups the results based on the specified fields: label, level, and message. sort by size desc: Orders the output by message size in descending order, allowing for easy identification of the largest messages.
filter @message like "error" | stats count(*) as total by stacktrace | sort total desc

This query identifies the most frequent errors by filtering messages containing the term "error" and grouping them by their stacktrace. Here’s a breakdown of the command: filter @message like "error": Filters the log entries to include only those that contain the string "error". stats count(*) as total by stacktrace: Aggregates the filtered results by counting the occurrences of each unique stacktrace and labeling the count as total. sort total desc: Sorts the results by the total count in descending order, making it easy to spot the most recurring exceptions.
for i in {1..10}; do npm run test test/index.test.ts; done
documents.s: Running a Test Multiple Times in Sequence

documents.t: This command executes a specific test script in your project multiple times in succession. It is useful when you need to validate the stability of the test or ensure consistent results over several runs. Below is a breakdown of the command: for i in {1..10}: This loop iterates 10 times, where i takes values from 1 to 10. npm run test test/index.test.ts: Runs the specified test file (index.test.ts) using the npm command, which is common in Node.js projects. done: Marks the end of the loop, causing the test to be run again until the loop completes all 10 iterations. This approach can be applied when conducting repetitive tests for reliability purposes or to observe any fluctuations in performance across multiple runs.
npm run users users.txt | tee audit_$(date +'%Y%m%d%H%M%S').txt

This command runs a task in a Node.js environment: processing user imports. It then captures the output of the user import process into a timestamped file for auditing purposes. Below is a detailed breakdown of the command: npm run users users.txt: Runs the users script, passing users.txt as an argument. This script likely handles the import or processing of users from the provided file. | tee: Pipes the output of the users command and writes it both to the console and to the specified file. audit_import_users_$(date +'%Y%m%d%H%M%S').txt: Creates a log file named with a timestamp (in the format YYYYMMDDHHMMSS), storing the output for later review or auditing. The date command dynamically generates the timestamp to ensure each audit file has a unique name. This approach ensures that user imports are tracked and verifiable, which is critical for auditing and troubleshooting in production environments.
grep -r "SOME_KEYWORK_HERE" . --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude=package-lock.json

This command searches for a specific string (in this case, "SOME_KEYWORK_HERE") recursively throughout the current directory, while explicitly ignoring specific directories and files to avoid unnecessary noise. Below is a breakdown of the command: grep -r "SOME_KEYWORK_HERE" .: Uses the grep tool to search recursively (-r) for the text "SOME_KEYWORK_HERE" starting from the current directory (.). --exclude-dir=node_modules: Excludes the node_modules folder from the search, which is crucial for performance as it prevents scanning thousands of library files. --exclude=package-lock.json: Excludes the package-lock.json file, ensuring that the results focus on your actual source code usage rather than dependency definitions. This is extremely useful when refactoring or checking where a specific library or variable is referenced in your codebase, ensuring clean results by ignoring generated or dependency-heavy files.
Claude Code is Anthropic's official CLI coding agent. It runs in your terminal, reads your files, edits code, runs commands, and can complete multi-step tasks autonomously.
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code You need an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in your environment. Set it in your shell profile: export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your_api_key_here
claude This opens an interactive session in your current directory. Claude can read, edit, and create files from here.
claude "Fix the failing tests in src/" Pass a prompt directly to run a single task without entering the interactive mode.
claude --continue Resumes the most recent conversation with its full context.
claude --resume Shows a list of recent sessions so you can pick one to continue.

Flag What it does --continue Resume the last conversation --resume Pick a past conversation to resume --model <id> Choose a specific Claude model --add-dir <path> Add an extra directory to the context --allowedTools <tools> Restrict which tools Claude can use --output-format json Print the final response as JSON (useful for scripts) --verbose Show detailed logs of what Claude is doing

Command What it does /help Show all available commands /clear Clear the conversation history /compact Summarize the conversation to save context space /model Switch to a different model /add-dir <path> Add a directory to the current session /allowed-tools Show or change which tools are enabled /memory Edit Claude's persistent memory /status Show account and session information /cost Show token usage and estimated cost for the session /exit Exit Claude Code
claude "The login endpoint returns 500 when the password is wrong. Fix it." Claude reads the relevant files, applies the fix, and shows a diff.
cd my-project claude "Add pagination to the /posts endpoint. Use limit and offset query params." Claude explores the codebase, edits the right files, and can run tests to verify the change.
claude "Explain how the auth middleware works" Claude reads the code and answers without making any changes.

Claude Code supports Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. They extend Claude with extra tools like database access, browser control, or external APIs. To add an MCP server: claude mcp add To list configured servers: claude mcp list
OpenCode is an open-source terminal coding agent. It connects to many AI providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and local models via Ollama), reads your files, edits code, and runs terminal commands.
npm install -g opencode-ai Or with a shell script: curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash
opencode This opens an interactive session in your current directory.
opencode "Add error handling to the fetch calls in src/api.ts" Pass a prompt directly to run a task without entering the interactive mode.

OpenCode uses a config file at ~/.config/opencode/config.json. Set the provider and model you want to use: { "provider": "anthropic", "model": "claude-opus-4-8" } For Anthropic, set your API key: export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your_api_key_here
Start Ollama with your model running, then launch OpenCode pointing to it: opencode --provider ollama --model qwen3:14b Or launch it directly from Ollama: ollama launch opencode

FROM pg_settings: Queries the pg_settings system catalog, which contains configuration parameters for the PostgreSQL instance. WHERE name LIKE '%autovacuum%': Filters the settings to include only those whose names contain the substring autovacuum. documents.s: Check Index Status and Safe Drop

documents.t: This sequence of commands is used to verify the status of an index, remove it without locking the table, and configure session timeouts. SELECT ... FROM pg_index: Checks the health of the index new_cart_id_idx. indisvalid: Returns true if the index is valid for queries. If false, the index creation likely failed. indisready: Shows if the index is ready for inserts/updates. DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY: Removes the index without locking the table against writes. This is the recommended way to drop indexes in production environments. SET statement_timeout = '300s': Sets a safety limit for the current session, ensuring that subsequent queries are aborted if they take longer than 300 seconds (5 minutes). SHOW statement_timeout: Verifies that the timeout configuration has been applied correctly. Use this workflow when managing indexes on live databases to avoid downtime or performance degradation.
SELECT pid, usename, state, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state != 'idle';

This query retrieves a list of currently running processes in the database, excluding idle connections. FROM pg_stat_activity: Queries the system view that shows information related to server processes. state != 'idle': Filters out connections that are currently doing nothing, focusing only on active, running, or blocked queries. pid: The process ID, useful if you need to terminate a specific query using pg_terminate_backend(pid). query: Displays the actual SQL text being executed. This is an essential command for troubleshooting performance issues, identifying stuck queries, or monitoring real-time database load.
-- get the values of an enum SELECT * FROM pg_enum WHERE enumtypid = 'enum_order_products_status'::regtype ORDER BY enumsortorder;

This query retrieves the list of valid labels defined for a specific ENUM type, preserving their defined order. FROM pg_enum: Queries the system catalog that stores specific information about enum types and their labels. 'enum_order_products_status'::regtype: Dynamically looks up the internal Object ID (OID) for the enum named enum_order_products_status. This is safer and easier than manually finding the numeric ID. ORDER BY enumsortorder: Ensures the results are returned in the logical order defined in the enum (e.g., PENDING, PROCESSING, COMPLETED), rather than alphabetical order. Use this when you need to programmatically verify the allowed values for a specific status column or debug schema inconsistencies.
WHERE 'INFO' = ANY(tags);
documents.s: Retrieve Rows Containing a Specific Tag (Method 1)

documents.t: This condition checks if the value 'INFO' exists inside the array column tags. 'INFO': The tag we want to search for. = ANY(tags): Tests whether 'INFO' matches at least one element of the array tags. This method is useful when you want to see if a single value is present inside an array column.
WHERE tags @> ARRAY['INFO'];
documents.s: Retrieve Rows Containing a Specific Tag (Method 2)

documents.t: This condition checks if the array column tags contains the array ['INFO']. tags: The array column. @>: The "contains" operator in PostgreSQL. ARRAY['INFO']: An array with one element, 'INFO'. This method is useful to test if the array column includes all values from another array. In this case, it checks if tags contains 'INFO'.
SELECT * FROM my_table WHERE data->>'identifier' = '12345';
documents.s: Retrieve rows where identifier is in the JSON root

documents.t: This SQL query finds rows where the JSON column data has a key identifier in the top level and its value is '12345'. SELECT *: returns all columns for matching rows. FROM my_table: use your table named my_table. data->>'identifier': extracts the value of identifier as text from the jsonb column data. = '12345': compares the extracted text with '12345'. This query is useful when identifier is stored at the top level of the JSON object.
SELECT * FROM my_table WHERE data @> '{"identifier":"12345"}'::jsonb;
documents.s: Use JSON containment to check key/value

documents.t: This query checks if the JSON object contains the pair "identifier": "12345". data @> ...: the @> operator tests whether the left JSON contains the right JSON. '{"identifier":"12345"}'::jsonb: a small JSON object on the right, cast to jsonb. Use this when you want to check that the JSON contains a given key and value. It also works well when you check multiple keys at once.
Example JSON row: { "person": { "identifier": "12345", "type": "passport" } } Query: SELECT * FROM my_table WHERE data->'person'->>'identifier' = '12345';
documents.s: When identifier is inside a nested object

documents.t: This finds identifier inside the nested object person. data->'person': returns the JSON object at key person. ->>'identifier': then gets the identifier value as text. Compare with '12345' as before. Use this when your JSON groups data inside objects (like person, owner, user, etc.).
SELECT * FROM my_table WHERE data #>> '{person,identifier}' = '12345';
documents.s: Use path extraction with #>> for nested keys

documents.t: #>> reads a text value using a path array. '{person,identifier}': the path — first person, then identifier. #>> returns text directly, so you can compare with =. This is a compact way to reach deep keys without chaining multiple -> operators.
SELECT * FROM my_table WHERE data->>'identifier' ILIKE '123%';

This does a case-insensitive match and finds identifiers that start with 123. ILIKE works like LIKE but ignores case. '123%' means "starts with 123". Use this for searches where you only know part of the identifier or want case-insensitive matches.
SELECT * FROM my_table WHERE (data->>'identifier')::bigint > 1000;
documents.s: Numeric comparison (when the JSON value is numeric)

documents.t: This converts the identifier text to a number and compares it. (data->>'identifier')::bigint: cast the extracted text to a big integer. > 1000: numeric comparison. Only use this when the JSON value is a number or a numeric string. If the cast fails, the query will error.
SELECT * FROM my_table WHERE jsonb_path_exists(data, '$.identifier ? (@ == "12345")');

This uses jsonpath to check if identifier equals "12345". jsonb_path_exists(data, '<path>'): returns true if the path condition matches. $.identifier: the identifier at the root. ? (@ == "12345"): a filter that checks equality. jsonpath is powerful for complex conditions and arrays.

-- fast equality on the identifier value CREATE INDEX idx_my_table_identifier ON my_table ((data->>'identifier')); -- general jsonb index for containment and other jsonb queries CREATE INDEX idx_my_table_data_gin ON my_table USING gin (data);
documents.s: Create indexes to speed up searches

documents.t: The first index is an expression (btree) on data->>'identifier'. Use it when you run many equality queries like = '12345'. The second index is a GIN index on the whole jsonb column. It helps queries that use @> and other jsonb operators. Create the index that fits your common queries. You can have both if needed.

Replace my_table and data with your real table and column names. Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to check query plans and see if indexes are used. Test casting and ILIKE carefully to avoid errors or slow queries. If you want, I can give a small full example with CREATE TABLE, some INSERT rows, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE for one query.
The Web Speech API is a tool that lets your browser "speak" text out loud. This is very useful for accessibility or language learning apps.

Here is a common way to use it in a React component: // import React from 'react'; const playAudio = (e: React.MouseEvent, word: string): void => { e.stopPropagation(); // Avoid parent events // Check if the browser supports speech if ('speechSynthesis' in window) { const utterance = new SpeechSynthesisUtterance(word); // Configuration utterance.lang = 'en-US'; // Set the language utterance.rate = 0.9; // Speed (0.9 is a bit slower) // Start speaking window.speechSynthesis.speak(utterance); } else { console.warn("Speech is not supported in this browser."); } };

e.stopPropagation(): This is important in React. It stops the click from "bubbling up" to other elements. 'speechSynthesis' in window: This check is necessary because some old browsers cannot speak. new SpeechSynthesisUtterance(word): This creates the "message" or the "object" that contains the text. utterance.rate: This controls the speed. A value of 1.0 is normal speed. Using 0.9 makes it easier to understand. window.speechSynthesis.speak(): This is the final command that tells the computer to start the audio.
To support: When a program is able to run a specific feature. Clarity: How easy it is to hear or understand something. Slightly: A little bit. To prevent: To stop something from happening.
This document contains useful Git commands that streamline your workflow and help you manage your repositories effectively.
git ls-files | grep -v 'lock' | grep -v 'svg' | xargs wc -l
documents.s: Count Lines of Code Excluding Certain File Types

documents.t: This command counts the number of lines of code in your Git repository, excluding files with the extensions .lock and .svg. Here’s a breakdown of the command: git ls-files: Lists all tracked files in the repository. grep -v 'lock': Filters out any files that contain the string "lock". grep -v 'svg': Further filters out any files that contain the string "svg". xargs wc -l: Passes the remaining files to the wc command, which counts the number of lines in each file.
git fetch -p && for branch in $(git for-each-ref --format '%(refname) %(upstream:track)' refs/heads | awk '$2 == "[gone]" {sub("refs/heads/", "", $1); print $1}'); do git branch -D $branch; done
documents.s: Remove Branches That Have Already Been Pushed

documents.t: This command removes local branches that have already been deleted from the remote repository. Here’s how it works: git fetch -p: Fetches the latest changes from the remote repository and prunes (deletes) any remote-tracking branches that no longer exist. git for-each-ref --format '%(refname) %(upstream:track)' refs/heads: Lists all local branches along with their upstream tracking information. awk '$2 == "[gone]": Filters for branches whose upstream branches are gone (deleted). sub("refs/heads/", "", $1): Removes the refs/heads/ prefix from the branch names. git branch -D $branch: Deletes the local branch.
git reset --soft HEAD~1

This command undoes the last commit in your Git repository without removing the changes from the staging area. Here’s a breakdown of the command: git reset --soft HEAD~1: Moves the current branch pointer back by one commit, retaining all changes made in that commit in the staging area. This allows you to make further modifications or commit again without losing any work.
git reset

This command un-stages all files that were added to the staging area using git add. Here’s a breakdown of the command: git reset: Resets the staging area to match the last commit, effectively removing all files from the staging area while keeping the changes in the working directory. This allows you to modify the files further before staging them again or committing them.
This document provides useful commands for Git to compare differences between branches, file names, and remote references.
git --no-pager diff branch1..branch2

This command shows the full content differences (diffs) between two specific branches. Here’s a breakdown of the command: git diff: The primary command used to show changes between commits, commit and working tree, etc. branch1..branch2: Specifies the two tips to compare. It shows what you would see if you were looking at branch2 and comparing it back to branch1.
git --no-pager diff --name-only branch1..branch2

This query suppresses the code diffs and lists only the names of the files that have changed. Below is a breakdown of the command: --name-only: An option that instructs Git to show only the names of changed files, omitting the contextual diff (the actual lines of code). branch1..branch2: The source and target branches for the comparison.
git --no-pager diff --stat branch1..branch2

This command provides a summary of changes, showing which files changed and how many lines were added or removed. The following components detail the functionality: --stat: Generates a diffstat. It displays a histogram of insertions and deletions for each file, giving a quick overview of the magnitude of changes. branch1..branch2: The range of branches being compared.
git --no-pager diff origin/development..origin/feature

This command compares the state of branches as they exist on the remote repository (e.g., GitHub or GitLab) without needing to check them out locally. origin/development: References the development branch on the remote named origin. origin/feature: References a specific feature branch on the remote. This is useful for code reviews or verifying what will change before merging a remote branch.
git --no-pager diff branch1..branch2

This command outputs the diff directly to the terminal (stdout) without opening a pagination tool (like less or vi). git --no-pager: A global option that tells Git not to pipe the output into a pager. This is useful for scripts or when you want to scroll through the output in your terminal history. diff branch1..branch2: The standard comparison command executed after the pager is disabled.
git commit --amend -m "SOME_COMMENT"
documents.s: Amending the Last Git Commit Message

documents.t: This command modifies the most recent commit in your Git repository by changing its commit message. Here’s a breakdown of the command: git commit --amend: This option allows you to modify the last commit. It can be used to edit the commit message or to add changes to the commit. -m "some comment": This flag specifies the new commit message. Replace "some comment" with your desired message to reflect the changes made. Using this command is particularly useful for correcting typos or adding additional information to the commit message without creating a new commit.

> [!NOTE] > Useful information that users should know, even when skimming content. > [!TIP] > Helpful advice for doing things better or more easily. > [!IMPORTANT] > Key information users need to know to achieve their goal. > [!WARNING] > Urgent info that needs immediate user attention to avoid problems. > [!CAUTION] > Advises about risks or negative outcomes of certain actions. The background color is `#ffffff` for light mode and `#000000` for dark mode.

This section provides Markdown formatting blocks for presenting different types of notes and warnings in documentation. Each block has a specific purpose and helps guide readers to the most relevant information. Here’s a breakdown: [!NOTE]: Indicates useful information that is relevant but non-critical. [!TIP]: Offers practical advice or shortcuts for enhanced efficiency. [!IMPORTANT]: Highlights essential information to ensure user success. [!WARNING]: Emphasizes critical information to prevent user errors. [!CAUTION]: Warns users about potential negative consequences.

In documentation using these blocks, the background color adapts based on the mode: Light Mode: Background color is #ffffff. Dark Mode: Background color is #000000. These blocks are particularly helpful for creating structured and user-friendly documentation, allowing readers to quickly identify key points and actionable advice.
For additional Markdown formatting options, see the GitHub documentation.

<details> <summary>CLICK ME</summary> ... </details> This section can be expanded or collapsed, providing a clean way to organize content. The details HTML tag is beneficial for enhancing readability and user experience by allowing users to toggle the visibility of additional information.

The usage of the details tag is straightforward. Here’s how it functions: <details>: This tag creates a disclosure widget from which the user can obtain additional information or controls. <summary>: This tag specifies a summary or heading for the details content. It is always visible, serving as a toggle for the expandable section. The content within the details tag will be hidden by default and can be revealed by clicking on the summary.

This repository is dedicated to storing and optimizing code snippets and useful commands that enhance my development workflow. Here, you will find a collection of utilities aimed at streamlining repetitive tasks and improving productivity in various programming environments. Note: This documentation is created with the assistance of ChatGPT and similar tools.
documents.s: Welcome to My Essential Dev Utils Repository

documents.t: This repository is a personal collection and may contain errors. Use the content at your own discretion and responsibility.

Essential development utilities refer to a curated set of code snippets and commands that serve as invaluable resources for developers. By organizing these utilities, I aim to create a comprehensive reference that simplifies the development process, enabling quicker and more efficient coding.

Code Snippets: A collection of reusable code snippets categorized by programming languages and frameworks. Useful Commands: A compilation of commands that can be executed in various development environments to automate tasks and improve efficiency. To get started, explore the sections for specific code snippets or useful commands. You can also check the best practices to learn how to maximize the effectiveness of your development utilities. Thank you for visiting!
pip3 cache purge python3 -m venv cache_venv source cache_venv/bin/activate pip install package
documents.s: Clearing the Pip Cache and Installing a Package in a Virtual Environment

documents.t: This set of commands purges the existing cache for pip and installs a Python package in a newly created virtual environment. Below is a detailed breakdown of each command: pip3 cache purge: Clears all cached packages stored by pip to free up space or ensure a fresh installation of dependencies. python3 -m venv cache_venv: Creates a new Python virtual environment named cache_venv to isolate dependencies for the project. source cache_venv/bin/activate: Activates the virtual environment, switching the terminal to use the isolated Python and pip versions within the environment. pip install package: Installs the specified Python package (replace package with the actual package name) in the activated virtual environment. This approach ensures a clean environment for managing Python dependencies, avoiding conflicts with system-wide packages or previously cached versions.
pip freeze > requirements.txt pip install -r requirements.txt
documents.s: Export and Install Python Package Dependencies

documents.t: These commands manage the dependencies of your Python project by exporting and reinstalling packages. Here’s a breakdown of the command sequence: pip freeze > requirements.txt: Creates a requirements.txt file that lists all currently installed packages and their versions. This file allows for easy recreation of the same environment by specifying exact versions. pip install -r requirements.txt: Installs the packages listed in requirements.txt to replicate the project environment on another machine or after a fresh setup. This approach is particularly useful for ensuring consistency across development environments, allowing team members or production systems to install identical dependencies as in the original setup.
let spy: jest.SpyInstance; beforeEach(() => { spy = jest .spyOn(someModule, "someMethod") .mockImplementation(defaultValue); }); afterEach(() => { spy.mockRestore(); });
documents.s: Using Jest Spy Instances for Testing

documents.t: This code snippet demonstrates how to use Jest's spy functions to mock and restore functionality during testing. Below is a detailed explanation of each part: let spy: jest.SpyInstance; Declares a variable spy to hold the spy instance. This ensures the spy can be accessed and restored later in the test lifecycle. beforeEach(() => { ... }); Defines a setup function that runs before each test case. Inside this block: jest.spyOn: Creates a spy for the someMethod method of the someModule object. .mockImplementation: Temporarily replaces the original implementation with the defaultValue function for controlled testing. afterEach(() => { ... }); Defines a cleanup function that runs after each test case. It calls spy.mockRestore() to: Remove the mocked implementation. Restore the original method behavior, ensuring no side effects persist between test cases.

Using this approach ensures isolation between tests and prevents unintended interactions with the original implementation of someMethod. It is particularly useful for testing code that depends on specific configurations or behaviors provided by the mocked method.
To track the logs when a Node.js instance encounters a crash, consider monitoring the following types of errors: JavaScript heap out of memory uncaughtException unhandledRejection
documents.s: Logs When a Node.js Instance Crashes

documents.t: These logs indicate potential issues with the Node.js instance that may lead to application crashes or unexpected behavior. Here’s an overview of each type of error: JavaScript heap out of memory: This error occurs when the application exceeds the available memory heap, causing it to crash. uncaughtException: This error occurs when an unhandled exception is thrown in the Node.js process, which can lead to the termination of the process. unhandledRejection: This error happens when a promise rejection is not properly handled, potentially leading to application instability.

To handle these errors and ensure the application continues running smoothly, you can add appropriate event listeners in your Node.js application: process.on('uncaughtException', (err) => { console.error('Uncaught exception:', err); // Handle the exception appropriately }); process.on('unhandledRejection', (reason, promise) => { console.error('Unhandled rejection:', reason); // Handle the rejection appropriately }); process.on('SIGUSR2', () => { console.log('JavaScript heap out of memory detected.'); // Handle memory-related errors appropriately }); These handlers allow you to log, manage, and respond to errors, improving the reliability of your Node.js application.
// src/libs/auth.ts export const validateToken = (token: string): Promise<string> => { ... };

Complete example of a test: jest.mock("../../../../src/libs/auth"); import { validateToken } from "../../../../src/libs/auth"; const mockValidateToken = validateToken as jest.Mock; describe("given a validateToken function", () => { beforeEach(() => { mockValidateToken.mockReturnValueOnce(Promise.resolve(userExample())); }); afterEach(() => { mockValidateToken.mockClear(); }); it("should return mocked user data", async () => { const result = await validateToken("eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9"); expect(result).toEqual({ name: "Søren Kierkegaard" }); }); });
Aider is a terminal-based coding assistant that connects to an LLM and edits your local files directly. It works with Git, tracks what files you add to the chat, and commits changes automatically.
pip install aider-install aider-install Or with pipx: pipx install aider-chat
aider By default, Aider looks for an OPENAI_API_KEY or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in your environment. To use a local model with Ollama, see the section below.

Start Ollama with your model running, then launch Aider pointing to it: aider --model ollama/qwen3:14b Use --edit-format whole when the model struggles to produce clean diffs — it tells Aider to rewrite the full file instead: aider --model ollama/qwen3:14b --edit-format whole
Aider only edits files you explicitly add. You can add them at startup: aider src/main.py src/utils.py Or inside the session with the /add command: /add src/main.py

Command What it does /add <file> Add a file to the chat so Aider can read and edit it /drop <file> Remove a file from the chat /ls List files currently in the chat /diff Show the last diff Aider produced /undo Undo the last Git commit Aider made /run <cmd> Run a shell command and share the output with the model /ask <question> Ask a question without making any edits /clear Clear the chat history /exit Exit Aider

Flag What it does --model <name> Choose the model to use --edit-format whole Rewrite full files instead of producing diffs --no-auto-commits Disable automatic Git commits --yes Skip confirmation prompts --watch-files Watch files for changes and sync them to the chat --read <file> Add a file as read-only context (Aider won't edit it)
aider src/api.py # Inside the session: > The /users endpoint returns a 500 when the user does not exist. Fix it. Aider reads the file, applies the fix, and commits it.
/ask What does the retry logic in src/client.py do? Aider answers without touching any files.

ollama run qwen3:14b This downloads the model (if it's not already available locally) and starts an interactive session with it.

To see which models are currently loaded into RAM and "running" on your Mac, open a new Terminal window and run: ollama ps Pressing Enter shows a table with the model name, its size, and how long it has been active in memory.
documents.s: Check Which Models Are Currently Running

documents.t: List all downloaded models (running or not): ollama list Unload a model from memory immediately (force Ollama to free the RAM instead of waiting for it to unload on its own): ollama stop qwen3:14b Replace qwen3:14b with the name of the model you want to stop. This document contains a useful query for New Relic to count transactions within a specified time frame and filter by application name.

SELECT count(*) FROM Transaction WHERE appName IN ('service-production') AND name LIKE '%queryName%' SINCE '2026-08-31T20:00 [America/Bogota]' UNTIL '2026-08-31T20:15 [America/Bogota]' FACET request.headers.origin

This query counts the number of transactions for a specific application within a defined time range. Here’s a breakdown of the command: SELECT count(*): Selects the count of all transactions that meet the specified criteria. FROM Transaction: Indicates the data source, which in this case is the Transaction event. WHERE appName IN ('service-production'): Filters the results to include only those transactions where the application name is service-production. AND name LIKE '%queryName%': Further filters the transactions to include only those whose names match the specified pattern (queryName). SINCE '2026-08-31T20:00 [America/Bogota]': Defines the start time for the query. UNTIL '2026-08-31T20:15 [America/Bogota]': Defines the end time for the query. FACET request.headers.origin: Groups the results by the origin header of the requests, allowing for insights into where the requests originated.

SELECT min(duration) as min_time, average(duration) as average_time, percentile(duration, 50, 90, 95, 99), max(duration) as max_time, stddev(duration) as stddev_time FROM Transaction WHERE appName = 'service-name' SINCE 4 hours ago -- SINCE 1 days ago -- SINCE 30 minutes ago

This query calculates detailed performance statistics regarding transaction durations (latency). It provides a comprehensive view of how fast or slow the application is responding. Here’s a breakdown of the command: min(duration) as min_time: Returns the shortest transaction duration found in the time window. average(duration) as average_time: Calculates the mean response time. percentile(duration, 50, 90, 95, 99): Displays the duration at various thresholds. For example, the 99th percentile indicates that 99% of requests were faster than this value (useful for spotting outliers). max(duration) as max_time: Returns the longest transaction duration (the slowest request). stddev(duration) as stddev_time: Calculates the standard deviation, which helps measure the consistency of the response times (a lower number means more consistent performance). WHERE appName = 'service-name': Limits the analysis to a specific service. SINCE 4 hours ago: Sets the time window for the analysis. The commented lines (--) show alternative common timeframes like 1 day or 30 minutes. This query is essential for analyzing application health, identifying performance degradation, and validating Service Level Agreements (SLAs).
You can access it at: ScriptHub, which is a curated collection of valuable scripts aimed at streamlining development processes, automating tasks, and enhancing overall efficiency.

npx skills is a CLI tool for managing reusable Claude Code skills. Skills are prompt-based plugins that extend Claude Code's behavior — you can install them from public registries, link them globally, or share your own.
No install needed. Run directly with npx: npx skills --help Or install globally to use the skills command without npx: npm install -g skills
Downloads the skill into .agents/skills/ inside your project directory: npx skills add anthropics/skills --skill skill-creator
documents.s: Add a skill to the current project

documents.t: Downloads the skill into ~/.agents/skills/: npx skills add anthropics/skills --skill skill-creator -g Use -g when you want the skill available across all your projects.

Instead of copying, create a symlink from the global install into your project's Claude skills folder: ln -s ~/.agents/skills/skill-creator ~/.claude/skills/skill-creator This way the skill stays up to date when you update the global copy, and you avoid duplicating files.
documents.s: Link a global skill into a project

documents.t: If your project keeps skills in a ./skills/ directory at the repo root, you can link the whole folder at once: ln -s ./skills ./.claude/skills This makes every skill in ./skills/ available to Claude Code without copying anything. Useful when the team manages skills directly in the repo and everyone should get all of them automatically.

This document outlines how to manage AWS credentials for different environments using the AWS CLI and Terraform.

File: ~/.aws/credentials Command: aws configure [staging] aws_access_key_id = KEY-STAGING aws_secret_access_key = SECRET-AWS [production] aws_access_key_id = KEY-PRODUCTION aws_secret_access_key = SECRET-AWS

This configuration file stores the AWS access keys for different environments. Here’s a breakdown of the sections: [staging]: Defines the credentials for the staging environment. aws_access_key_id: The access key ID for the staging environment. aws_secret_access_key: The secret access key for the staging environment. [production]: Defines the credentials for the production environment. aws_access_key_id: The access key ID for the production environment. aws_secret_access_key: The secret access key for the production environment.
To switch between the defined profiles, you can set the AWS_PROFILE environment variable. Use the following commands: Staging​ export AWS_PROFILE=staging
export AWS_PROFILE=production

These commands set the AWS_PROFILE variable to specify which set of credentials to use when interacting with AWS services. By changing this variable, you can easily switch between different environments (staging and production) without modifying the credentials file.
rm -rf .terraform .terraform.lock.hcl

This command removes the Terraform cache and lock file to prevent potential conflicts in your environment. Here’s a breakdown of the command: rm -rf: A command used to remove files and directories forcefully and recursively. .terraform: This directory contains Terraform's cached state files and configurations. .terraform.lock.hcl: This file locks the provider versions and configurations for the Terraform project. Removing these files may help resolve issues related to outdated or conflicting state information.
terraform init && terraform plan

This command performs two essential steps in managing infrastructure with Terraform: initializing the working directory and generating an execution plan. Here's a breakdown of the command: terraform init: Prepares the working directory by downloading and installing any necessary provider plugins and setting up the backend for state management. terraform plan: Generates an execution plan that shows what actions Terraform will take to apply the current configuration, without making any changes to your infrastructure. This sequence ensures that the Terraform environment is correctly configured and provides an overview of the potential modifications before execution.
terraform apply

This command applies the Terraform configuration by creating or updating infrastructure based on the configuration files. Below is a breakdown of the command: terraform apply: Executes the actions specified in the Terraform configuration files. This command will prompt for approval before making any changes unless the -auto-approve flag is used. Before running this command, ensure the Terraform configuration has been initialized with terraform init. The command generates a plan, detailing the resources to be added, modified, or destroyed, allowing for a careful review before proceeding with the changes.
find . -name ".terraform" -type d -exec rm -rf {} +

This command recursively deletes all directories named .terraform from the current directory and its subdirectories. Here’s a breakdown of the command: find .: Searches the current directory and all its subdirectories. -name ".terraform": Specifies that only directories with the name .terraform will be targeted. -type d: Ensures that only directories are included in the search. -exec rm -rf {} +: Executes the rm -rf command to remove the found directories recursively. The {} is replaced by the directory paths found by the find command.
find . -name ".terraform.lock.hcl" -type f -exec rm -f {} +

This command recursively deletes all .terraform.lock.hcl files from the current directory and its subdirectories. Here’s a breakdown of the command: find .: Searches the current directory and all its subdirectories. -name ".terraform.lock.hcl": Specifies that only files named .terraform.lock.hcl will be targeted. -type f: Ensures that only files are included in the search. -exec rm -f {} +: Executes the rm -f command to forcefully remove the found files. The {} is replaced by the file paths found by the find command.

Use the causative verbs have, get, make and let to say who causes an action, and how strong the force is.

A causative verb says that one person or thing causes another person or thing to do something. Each verb has a different degree of force. Verb Force Structure Example make strong (no choice) make + person + base verb The manager made us redo the report. have neutral (a request or an assigned task) have + person + base verb I had the intern book the room. get needs a little persuasion get + person + to + base verb I got my colleague to review my code. let gives permission let + person + base verb My boss let me work from home.
The policeman made him stop the car. After checking all my documents, the officer let me enter the building.

Say that something is possible using modals + base verb and adverbs of uncertainty.

Use a modal with the base form of the verb to say that something is possible. You are not sure. You only say it can happen. Modal Structure Example can / could subject + can/could + base verb This protocol can decrease hospital infections a lot. may / might subject + may/might + base verb They may agree with our proposition. The modals are the same for all subjects: I, you, he, she, it, we, they. Which modal is stronger? For possibility, can, could, may and might are close in meaning. Might and may often show more doubt. Could is very common and safe in meetings.

You can also use adverbs. They show that you are not 100% sure. Adverb Position Example Maybe start of the sentence Maybe they'll like our new hygiene protocol. Perhaps start of the sentence Perhaps they'll like our new protocol. Possibly between will and the verb They'll possibly ask for statistics about our research. maybe vs may be Maybe (one word) is an adverb: Maybe we can finish today. May be (two words) is a modal + verb: The client may be late. One modal per verb Maybe we could… is fine and polite. But never put two modals together (we might could). Keep one modal per verb. See general modal rules. Spanish speakers Do not use to after may or might. Say We might go, not We might to go. Also, English does not need that after maybe (quizás que): say Maybe we can finish, not Maybe that we can finish.

You must have enjoyed the trip. may / might / could be puede que sea / esté They might be busy right now. may / might / could have + past participle puede que haya... They could have been busy yesterday. can't be no puede ser (imposible) That can't be the right number. can't have + past participle no puede haber... I can't have missed the bus. probable probable It is probable that the server is down. impossible imposible It is impossible to finish today.

Present Past Team chat Ana isn't answering. She might be in a meeting. The client is silent. They could be reading the contract. The build is green. The tests must be passing. That can't be the right file. It is too small. Incident review The page crashed at 9:00. Someone must have deployed a change. The email may have gone to spam. The developer can't have seen the alert. His phone was off. 💬 Missing report Marta: Where is the sales report? Pablo sent it yesterday. Luis: It might have gone to spam. Marta: It can't have gone to spam. I checked. Luis: Then he must have forgotten to send it. Or he could have used the wrong address. Email to a colleague Hi Tom, I did not get your message. It may have been a connection problem. You must have been very busy this week. Let's talk on Monday. Best, Laura

❌ Wrong ✅ Correct Why You must enjoyed traveling. You must have enjoyed traveling. Past guess: must + have + past participle. They might busy right now. They might be busy right now. Use be before an adjective. She mustn't be happy about getting fired. She can't be happy about getting fired. can't expresses "impossible". I can't missed the bus. I can't have missed the bus. Past: can't + have + past participle. They may been busy yesterday. They may have been busy yesterday. Do not forget have.

The lights are on. Someone ______ (must / be) in the office. I do not know where Sam is. He ______ (might / be) at lunch. The server crashed. A developer ______ (must / change) the settings. She just got fired. She ______ (can't / be) happy.
Rewrite each sentence with the modal in brackets. I am sure that the client enjoyed the demo. (must) Maybe the team was busy yesterday. (might) It is impossible that I missed the call. (can't)
A colleague is late. Make three guesses about why with must, might and can't. Your website is down. Say what probably happened in the past using must have and could have.
You are sure that something is impossible in the past. Which one is correct? I mustn't have missed the bus.I can't have missed the bus.I can't missed the bus.

Show answers A. must be might be must have changed can't be B. The client must have enjoyed the demo. The team might have been busy yesterday. I can't have missed the call. C. Answers vary. Check that present guesses use a base verb and past guesses use have + past participle.

Must = sure it is true. May / might / could = maybe. Can't = sure it is impossible. Present: modal + base verb (must be, might be). Past: modal + have + past participle (must have been, might have gone). Use can't, not mustn't, for a negative guess.

I can choose between must, might and can't for a guess. I can form the past with modal + have + past participle. I know that mustn't is not used for impossible. I can explain a past problem at work with must have and could have. I can guess about a colleague's situation in a conversation.

Assumptions The class notes cover three ideas: the first conditional, phrases to discuss business options, and phrases to make suggestions. This page puts them together because you often use them in the same meeting.
Talk about a possible action and its likely result with If + present simple, will + base verb. Then use set phrases to discuss options and make suggestions.

The first conditional talks about a possible action and its likely result in the future. Structure If + present simple , will + base verb (condition) (result) Part Verb form Example Condition (if clause) present simple If the client signs the contract, Result (main clause) will + base verb we will deliver the order next month. Two ways to build it You can put the result first. Then you do not need a comma. If we finalize the project details today, we will assign tasks to the team tomorrow. We will assign tasks to the team tomorrow if we finalize the project details today. No will in the if clause Use the present simple after if, even when you talk about the future. Say If the client signs, not If the client will sign.

Use conditionals to compare options and their consequences. If we implement a workforce reduction plan, our company will be able to cope with the global recession. If we freeze hiring, we won't have to fire some of our best employees. If we do this, then the company will lose a great deal of talent. You can add then to the result to make it stronger: If we do this, then the company will lose…

Phrase Example What if ... What if we consider outsourcing overseas? An alternative ... An alternative could be stopping all salary increases and bonuses. How about ... How about we implement cost-cutting strategies?

Direct phrases I suggest ..., We suggest ... and Let's ... are direct and clear. Modals and question words soften a suggestion and sound more polite. Pattern Example You/We/They could + base verb We could move the deadline to Friday. You/We/They might (not) want to + base verb You might want to review the budget first. What/How about + verb-ing? How about reviewing it together? Why don't/doesn't + subject + base verb? Why don't we ask the client for more time? Why not + base verb? Why not start with a small pilot?

English Meaning / Spanish hint Example sentence sign the contract firmar el contrato If the client signs the contract, we will start next week. finalize finalizar, cerrar If we finalize the details today, we will assign tasks tomorrow. freeze hiring congelar las contrataciones If we freeze hiring, we will save money this year. cope with hacer frente a, sobrellevar The company will cope with the recession if it cuts costs. outsourcing subcontratación, externalizar What if we consider outsourcing overseas? cost-cutting reducción de costos How about we implement cost-cutting strategies? a great deal of una gran cantidad de We will lose a great deal of talent. an alternative una alternativa An alternative could be a smaller team.

Formal Informal Email to client Dear Ms. Lopez, If you sign the contract by Friday, we will deliver the order next month. If we receive the final specifications today, we will start the work on Monday. Best regards, Daniel Slack message If the tests pass today, we will deploy tomorrow morning. If you need help with the review, ping me and I will join the call. 💬 Budget meeting Manager: We need to reduce costs this quarter. What are our options? Sara: If we freeze hiring, we won't have to fire anyone. Tom: True, but if we do this, then the team will have too much work. Sara: What if we consider outsourcing the support tasks? Manager: Good idea. How about we ask two vendors for a quote? Team suggestions Let's review the plan on Monday. We could split the project into two phases. You might want to share the report before the meeting. Why don't we ask the client for feedback?

❌ Wrong ✅ Correct Why If the client will sign, we will deliver the order. If the client signs, we will deliver the order. No will in the if clause. If we freeze hiring, we don't have to fire anyone next month. If we freeze hiring, we won't have to fire anyone. Use will or won't in the result for a future consequence. If we will finalize the details, we assign tasks. If we finalize the details, we will assign tasks. Present simple in the if clause, will in the result. Why we don't ask the client? Why don't we ask the client? Question word order: auxiliary before subject. How about to implement a new plan? How about implementing a new plan? Use verb-ing after How about. Spanish speakers The idea is about the future, so many Spanish speakers add will after if (If the client will sign…). In English, never use will right after if in the first conditional. Use the present simple.

If the client ______ (sign) the contract, we ______ (deliver) the order next month. If we ______ (freeze) hiring, we ______ (not / have) to fire anyone. If we ______ (finalize) the details today, we ______ (assign) tasks tomorrow. If we ______ (set) the price too low, we ______ (lose) money.

Rewrite each sentence as a suggestion with the phrase in brackets. We should outsource the support tasks. (What if ...) Stop all salary increases for a year. (An alternative ...) We can ask the client for more time. (Why don't we ...?) You should review the budget first. (You might want to ...)
Your team has a tight deadline. Give two options using If … will …. Suggest a solution to a problem at work using What if, How about and Let's.
Choose the correct first conditional. If we will finalize the details, we assign tasks.If we finalize the details, we will assign tasks.If we finalized the details, we will assign tasks.

Show answers A. signs, will deliver freeze, won't have finalize, will assign set, will lose B. Possible answers: What if we outsource the support tasks? An alternative could be stopping all salary increases for a year. Why don't we ask the client for more time? You might want to review the budget first. C. Answers vary. Check that the if clause uses the present simple and the result uses will or won't.

First conditional = If + present simple, will + base verb. It talks about a possible future action and its likely result. Never use will in the if clause. Use What if, An alternative and How about to discuss business options. Use Let's, could, might want to, Why don't we and Why not to make suggestions.

I can write the structure from memory. I can give three workplace examples with If … will …. I know the difference between the zero conditional and the first conditional. I can suggest an option with What if, How about and An alternative. I can make a polite suggestion with could or might want to.
Use modal verbs (can, must, will, should, might) correctly in the present, future and past.

Modals are helper verbs. They add meaning such as ability, obligation, advice or possibility. They all follow the same five rules. # Rule Example 1 Modals do not change form for singular or plural subjects. She can help. They can help. 2 The verb after a modal is always in the base form. We should send the report. 3 A verb is attached to only one modal. We will be able to finish. 4 Present and future: modal + base verb. I can join the call now. 5 Past: modal + have + past participle. He should have called the client. Quick formula Present or future: modal + base verb Past: modal + have + past participle
Normal verbs add -s in the third person (she works). Modals never do. Correct: She can speak English. Wrong: She cans speak English.
The base form is the verb without to, -s, -ed or -ing. Correct: He must finish today. Wrong: He must finishes / to finish / finishing today.
You cannot put two modals together. Use a substitute expression for the second one. Wrong: We will can deliver on time. Correct: We will be able to deliver on time.

To talk about the past, use have + past participle after the modal. Modal Past form Example should should have + past participle You should have told me earlier. must must have + past participle The server must have crashed. might might have + past participle The email might have gone to spam. can't can't have + past participle She can't have forgotten the meeting. can in the past For ability in the past, use could (I could code at 12), not can have. Do not use to after a modal Do not say I must to go or She should to call. Use the base verb directly.

Present and future Past Stand-up I can review your pull request this afternoon. We will deploy after the tests pass. You should update the documentation. Post-mortem We should have added more tests. The deploy might have caused the error. Someone must have changed the configuration. 💬 Code review Ana: The page loads slowly. We should optimize the images. Leo: I can do that today. We will see a difference tomorrow. Ana: Great. We should have done it before the launch. Email to the team Hi all, You must complete the security training by Friday. If you have questions, you can ask HR. Thanks, Paula

❌ Wrong ✅ Correct Why She cans help you. She can help you. Modals never take -s. We should to send the report. We should send the report. No to after a modal. He must finishes today. He must finish today. Use the base form. We will can deliver on Monday. We will be able to deliver on Monday. Only one modal per verb. You should told me. You should have told me. Past: modal + have + past participle. Spanish speakers In Spanish, the second verb is an infinitive (puedo ir, debo ir, tengo que ir), so many learners add to in English too. After a modal there is no to: can go, must go, should go. Only have to and be able to include to.

Choose the correct form of the verb in brackets. She can ______ (speak) three languages. We should ______ (check) the numbers again. They might ______ (be) late for the meeting. You must ______ (show) your ID at the entrance.

Fix each sentence or change it to the past. He musts send the report today. We will can finish on time. I should call the client. (past: I did not call) The server must crash last night. (the speaker is sure)
Give three pieces of advice to a new colleague using should. Talk about a mistake in a past project using should have.
Choose the correct sentence. She should to call the client.She should calls the client.She should call the client.

Show answers A. speak check be show B. He must send the report today. We will be able to finish on time. I should have called the client. The server must have crashed last night. C. Answers vary. Check that the verb after should is in the base form, and that you use have + past participle for the past.

Modals do not change for singular or plural subjects. After a modal, always use the base form of the verb. One verb, one modal. Use be able to as a substitute. Present and future: modal + base verb. Past: modal + have + past participle.

I can list five modals. I never add -s or to after a modal. I can change a modal sentence to the past. I can use be able to instead of two modals together. I can use these rules with must for obligation and confident guesses.

Assumptions The class notes cover simple comparisons with comparative adjectives (-er than, more ... than, as ... as). This page adds less ... than, not as ... as and a short note on superlatives to make the topic complete.
Compare two people, tools or options using comparative adjectives and as + adjective + as.

Use a comparative adjective to show a difference between two things. Use as ... as to show they are equal. Type Structure Example Short adjective adjective + -er + than Frances is friendlier than Alice. Long adjective more + adjective + than Alice is more experienced than Frances. Equal as + adjective + as Frances is as motivated as the other nurses in the clinic. Less less + adjective + than This plan is less expensive than the old one. Not equal not as + adjective + as The old tool is not as fast as the new one. How to choose -er or more One syllable: add -er (fast, faster; cheap, cheaper). Two syllables ending in -y: change y to i and add -er (easy, easier; busy, busier). Two or more syllables: use more (experienced, more experienced; reliable, more reliable). Irregular adjectives good becomes better. bad becomes worse. far becomes further or farther.

Short adjective ending in one vowel + one consonant: double the consonant (big, bigger; hot, hotter). Adjective ending in -e: add -r (large, larger; safe, safer). Use than, not that Comparatives use than. With as ... as, do not use than. Correct: Our tool is faster than theirs. Correct: Our tool is as fast as theirs.
To compare three or more things, use the + adjective + -est or the most + adjective. Example: She is the most experienced developer on the team.

English Meaning / Spanish hint Example sentence friendly amable, simpático Frances is friendlier than Alice. experienced con experiencia Alice is more experienced than Frances. motivated motivado Frances is as motivated as the other nurses. reliable confiable This server is more reliable than the old one. affordable asequible, económico The new plan is cheaper and more affordable. compared to en comparación con Compared to last year, our sales are higher. the same as igual que The price is the same as last month. different from diferente de This version is different from the previous one.

Meeting Email Comparing two vendors Vendor A is cheaper than Vendor B. Vendor B is more experienced than Vendor A. Vendor A is as reliable as Vendor B, but its support is slower. Email to the team Hi team, The new dashboard is faster than the old one and easier to use. The new tool is not as expensive as I expected. Best, Maria 💬 Choosing a tool Carlos: Which tool is better for our team, Tool A or Tool B? Nina: Tool A is cheaper than Tool B, but Tool B is more flexible. Carlos: Is Tool A as easy to learn as Tool B? Nina: Yes, it is as easy as Tool B. I think Tool B is the better option.

❌ Wrong ✅ Correct Why Alice is more experienced that Frances. Alice is more experienced than Frances. Use than after a comparative. Frances is more friendlier than Alice. Frances is friendlier than Alice. Do not use more and -er together. This tool is more good than that one. This tool is better than that one. good is irregular: better. She is as motivated than the others. She is as motivated as the others. Use as ... as for equal. The server is more fast than the old one. The server is faster than the old one. Short adjectives take -er. Spanish speakers In Spanish we say más ... que and tan ... como. In English, the second word is than for difference and as for equality. Also, do not translate más bueno: use better.

Our new laptop is ______ (fast) than the old one. The manager is ______ (experienced) than the new intern. This report is ______ (good) than the last one. Sara is as ______ (motivated) ______ her teammates.

Rewrite each sentence with the word in brackets. Vendor A costs 500 dollars. Vendor B costs 700 dollars. (cheaper) The old process is slow. The new process is slow too. (as ... as) Tool B is very flexible. Tool A is not very flexible. (less)
Compare two tools you use at work (for example Slack and email). Compare your job today with your job two years ago.
Choose the correct sentence. Frances is more friendlier than Alice.Frances is friendlier than Alice.Frances is friendlier that Alice.

Show answers A. faster more experienced better motivated, as B. Possible answers: Vendor A is cheaper than Vendor B. The old process is as slow as the new process. Tool A is less flexible than Tool B. C. Answers vary. Check that you use than for differences and as ... as for equality.

Short adjectives: -er than (faster than). Long adjectives: more ... than (more experienced than). Equal: as ... as (as motivated as). Irregular: good, better; bad, worse. Never use more and -er together.

I can compare two options using -er than and more ... than. I can use as ... as to say two things are equal. I know the irregular forms better and worse. I use than and as correctly. I can compare two tools aloud in a meeting.
Use clues to explain a problem or a situation, with phrases like It seems that... and modals like must be, might be, could have, can't be.
A deduction is a conclusion from evidence. You do not know the answer for sure, but the clues point to it.

Use these phrases to say what you think the problem is: It seems that the server is out of memory. It's very likely that the database is slow. If you're seeing an error, and the logs are empty, it could mean that the service did not start. If the cable is connected, then the problem is the network card.

Use a modal followed by the infinitive without to. Modal Certainty Example must be very sure it is true It must be a permissions problem. might / may be possible It might be a bug in the new version. could be / could have possible (present or past) It could have failed during the deploy. can / can't be can: possible; can't: very sure it is not true It can't be the network. Other users are online. Present and past Present: must / might / could / can't + base verb (It must be a typo.) Past: must / might / could / can't + have + past participle (It must have been a typo.) Must for deduction Here must does not mean obligation. It means "I am almost sure". The opposite is can't, not mustn't. Do not use mustn't for deductions ❌ The file mustn't be on the server. ✅ The file can't be on the server.

English Meaning / Spanish hint Example sentence It seems that... Parece que... It seems that the cache is full. It's very likely that... Es muy probable que... It's very likely that the update broke the login. it could mean that... podría significar que... If the logs are empty, it could mean that nothing ran. evidence evidencia, pruebas What evidence do we have for that? clue pista The error message is a good clue. rule out descartar Let us rule out the network first. root cause causa raíz We still need to find the root cause. troubleshoot diagnosticar y resolver un problema I will troubleshoot the issue after lunch.

Support ticket After a deploy Internal note The customer cannot log in. It seems that the password reset email is not arriving. It might be in the spam folder, or the address could be wrong. It can't be a server outage, because other customers are fine. Slack message The page is blank since the release. It must be the new JavaScript bundle. It could have failed to load because of a cache problem. 💬 Troubleshooting call Sara: The app works for me, but not for the client. Tom: It must be something in their setup. It can't be our code. Sara: Maybe. It could be a firewall rule. Tom: If they are on a company network, and the port is closed, then the problem is the firewall.

❌ Wrong ✅ Correct Why It must to be a bug. It must be a bug. No to after a modal. It mustn't be the cable. It can't be the cable. Use can't for a negative deduction. It must be failed yesterday. It must have failed yesterday. Past deduction: modal + have + past participle. It could has failed. It could have failed. Always have, never has. It can be the network, I am sure. It must be the network. can is only possible. For strong certainty use must. Spanish speakers Spanish uses debe de ser for deduction, and debe also for obligation. In English they are separate: must be is a deduction and have to is an obligation. For the opposite deduction, say can't be (no puede ser), never mustn't be.

Use must, might, could or can't with the verb in brackets. The logs show an out-of-memory error. It ______ (be) a memory leak. (very sure) The office is dark and the door is locked. They ______ (be) here. (very sure it is not true) I am not sure why the build is slow. It ______ (be) the new dependency. (possible) The data is gone. Someone ______ (delete) it by mistake. (possible, past)

Your teammate says the website is slow. Give three deductions about the cause. Describe a problem you solved at work. Which clues helped you?
